c0011: ▸ The "Monthly Schedule" sheet repeats the grid for five weeks (31-day months do not fit in four), inherits the names from the "Weekly Schedule" and adds up each employee's total for the month. The weekly average is for planning only: under the FLSA each workweek stands alone — column J of each week is what counts. UK: the 48 h limit IS a 17-week average.
c0012: The 4 schedule alerts (columns K to N):
c0013: ▸ K · Rest between shifts: compares the END time of each day with the START time of the next, counting the shift that crosses midnight. It fires below 10 h, the "clopening" rule of predictive scheduling (Fair Workweek) laws. There is no federal rule: these are state or city laws (Oregon, Seattle, NYC, Chicago, Philadelphia and others), mostly for large chains. UK: 11 h, Working Time Regulations reg. 10. The threshold is cell Shifts!B3.
c0014: ▸ L · Weekly day off: federal law sets no mandatory day off. With zero days off in the week the alert is red; with one, amber (six days on: work on a 7th consecutive day of the workweek is premium pay in California, Labor Code §510(a); §§551-552 give one day's rest in seven). UK: 24 h off per week (WTR reg. 11).
c0015: ▸ M · Weekly hours: compares with the maximum in column J (green, 40 by default, the FLSA overtime threshold), not with a fixed 40: for a part-timer, type their scheduled hours and the alerts fire at 20. The grid runs Monday–Sunday, the same workweek as B3 of the "Time Log" in file 02 "Overtime Tracker & Time Log" (2 = Monday). If your payroll week starts on another day, change B3 there and read this grid accordingly.
c0016: ▸ N · Long shift: federal law sets no daily maximum for adults, so this is the kit's own rule: it fires above 10 h (threshold in Shifts!B2). It is the one that catches the double shift.
c0017: ▸ O and P · Minors: type Y in column O for anyone under 18 (the alert in file 07 "Employee Directory & Expiry Tracker" tells you as soon as you enter the date of birth). With Y, alert N drops to 8 h and P turns red on a NIGHT (N) or DOUBLE (DBL) shift and amber otherwise. The federal hour rules apply UNDER 16 (29 CFR 570.35): 8 h on a non-school day and no work after 7 PM (9 PM from June 1 to Labor Day), so a PM or SP shift that ends later is out too. For 16-17 there are no federal hour limits: check your state law (federal law bans only hazardous work such as meat slicers and dough mixers, 29 CFR 570.50-570.68). UK: young workers, 8 h a day, 40 h a week, no night work.
c0018: The shift table lives in the "Shifts" sheet:
c0019: ▸ Each code has its start time, its end time and its BREAK; the effective hours calculate themselves. Type times as clock times: 7:00 AM or 3:30 PM.
c0020: ▸ The SPLIT (SP) is 9 effective hours between 10:00 AM and 11:00 PM (13 h end to end minus a 4 h break); the DOUBLE (DBL) is 16 h and exists so the long-shift alert has something to catch.
c0021: ▸ V (vacation / PTO) and S (sick) are marked here with the same letters as in file 05 "PTO & Vacation Planner" and count 0 h. Holiday (H) and other leave (L) exist only in 05: in this schedule a day off is OFF.

c0023: ▸ Columns R to AR are HIDDEN: they are the helper calculation (hours, start time, end time and the 6 transitions between shifts). Unhide them if you want to audit an alert.
c0024: To edit a locked cell: Review → Unprotect Sheet (no password). Green cells are already editable without unprotecting anything.

c0129: ▸ Log clock-in, clock-out and BREAK. The break is what makes a split shift loggable: 10:00 AM → 11:00 PM with a 4 h break is 9 h worked, not 13. Use one row per person per day (two rows on the same date double-count weekly overtime).

c0132: ▸ This sheet has 300 rows: 30 people clocking in 6 days a week fill 180 per workweek; a team of 10 fits a whole month. Use one copy of the file per period (weekly or biweekly payroll: one per pay period). Each copy must hold WHOLE workweeks starting on the day in B3 of the "Time Log" (2 = Monday by default, the same week as the schedule in file 01). Keep a week that crosses months in one copy, or its overtime will be lost. Need more rows? Unprotect the sheet, insert them above row 304 and fill the formulas down: rows added below 304 are not counted.
c0134: ▸ FLSA, 29 U.S.C. 207(a)(1): overtime is every hour over 40 in the workweek, paid at 1.5× the regular rate. Federal law sets no yearly cap on overtime: the 80 h budget ("Monthly OT Summary", F3) is a kit rule you can change.
c0135: ▸ Some states add a daily rule (California: over 8 h in a day at 1.5×, over 12 h at 2×; Labor Code §510(a)). Type your state's daily threshold in F3 above the log; leave it blank for the federal rule only. UK: no legal overtime premium (gov.uk/overtime-your-rights).
c0136: ▸ That is why the multiplier is a green cell (D3 of the "Monthly OT Summary") and not a number inside a formula. Keep it at 1.5, the FLSA rate for non-exempt staff: California double time applies only over 12 h in a day and over 8 h on the 7th consecutive day of the workweek (Labor Code §510(a)), so do not set 2× for every hour; price those hours apart. Raise it only if your contract pays more than 1.5× on all overtime. Tipped staff: overtime is owed on the full minimum wage, not on the cash wage (29 CFR 531.60).
c0137: ▸ You may require overtime from non-exempt staff, but every hour worked must be paid, including overtime nobody approved (29 CFR 785.11-785.13).
c0139: ▸ Hours worked = clock-out − clock-in − break. Type times with a colon and AM/PM (9:00 AM, not 9): the drop-down rejects a bare 9, which Excel reads as nine DAYS and would leave the shift at 0.00 without warning.
c0140: ▸ Scheduled hours = the hours that person was SCHEDULED that day, preloaded at 8 for reference. Overtime does not depend on this column: it is calculated by the FLSA rule (hours over 40 in the workweek, plus the optional daily rule in F3).
c0141: ▸ OT type: Pre-approved · Manager request · Emergency / call-in · Not approved · Shift cover. The "Not approved" hours are counted in their own column of the summary because they are still payable.
c0142: ▸ Comp time does not exist for private employers: you cannot give time off instead of overtime pay (29 U.S.C. 207(o) covers only public agencies). So every overtime hour in this log is paid, including those marked "Not approved": if someone worked it, you owe it (29 CFR 785.11).
c0143: ▸ For a PART-TIME employee, extra hours are overtime only once the workweek passes 40 h; below that they are paid at the regular rate. Tag the hours a part-timer picks up for a colleague as "Shift cover" so you can find them later.
c0144: ▸ "Worked − scheduled hours (this copy)" carries a SIGN: it can be negative. The "OT hours (FLSA)" column of the log counts only the excess over 40 h in the workweek (and the daily rule if you set F3), so it does not see days below schedule. Use the balance to compare what you scheduled with what was worked; what you PAY as overtime is the log's OT column.
c0145: ▸ The "Alert" column of the log warns about the four ways to lose a shift silently: a time typed without the colon (9 instead of 9:00 AM), clock-in equal to clock-out, a break longer than the shift, and a name that is not in the "Monthly OT Summary" (SUMIF looks for the EXACT text: one extra space and that person shows zero).

What you legally owe for each OT hour is 1.5× the employee's regular rate of pay.

c0208: Why the labor cost traffic light works the way it does:
c0209: ▸ The traffic light does not say "EXCELLENT" on a blank sheet: with no sales AND no cost there is no verdict, and it tells you which of the two is missing. It does not congratulate an absurdly LOW ratio either: below 60% of your target it warns that payroll is probably still to be entered.
c0210: ▸ It does not fail fine dining: a fine dining restaurant at 38% is where it should be, and a fast casual at 38% is losing money. Both thresholds come from the reference table on that same sheet, which has all TEN concepts of BONUS-02 — hotel, pizzeria, ghost kitchen and ice cream shop included — with the same thresholds: the two files cannot give different verdicts on the same ratio.
c0211: ▸ The staffing forecast reasons per SERVICE. Eighty covers a day in two services are forty per service: sizing the shift with the eighty would double the team.
c0212: Note: this is a management tool, not payroll processing. Your actual employer taxes depend on your state, your insurer and your unemployment rate. Check with your payroll provider or accountant before you commit to anything.
c0225: Adjust to your state, insurer and unemployment rate. Estimate: about 10% = FICA 7.65% + FUTA/SUTA + workers' comp. UK: employer NI 15% above 5,000 a year + about 3% pension.
